articles.title: US firm gets $2.9bn sub deal after boss joins war study with Musk
articles.summary: Anduril said it would invest $3.7bn to develop shipyard that would build submarine parts.
articles.body:
Defence technology firm Anduril said it will invest $3.7bn to develop a new shipyard in the US state of Maryland and will build critical components for the United States Navy’s Virginia-class submarines, as Washington seeks to bolster its maritime defence capabilities.

California-based Anduril Industries confirmed on Tuesday it would invest in the submarine production plant, dubbed Arsenal-2, and will receive a $2.9bn US navy contract to manufacture submarine parts.

US President Donald Trump was set to unveil the project and announce a massive naval shipyard expansion in Baltimore, Maryland, on Tuesday afternoon.

Anduril is a defence technology firm whose co-founder, Palmer Luckey, is heading a new Defense Department project alongside technology billionaire and former top Trump adviser Elon Musk. Luckey and Musk were tapped by the Pentagon to lead Project Meridian, a newly-disclosed initiative focused on the future of warfare, including autonomous, AI-powered and maritime military capabilities.

Valued at nearly $117bn, Anduril specialises in uncrewed underwater vehicles and ocean vessels – or naval drones – designed for the US military and its allies.

The initiative was announced at Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s State of the Force address last week in Virginia, part of a 120-day study aimed at identifying new technology needed for next-generation US battlefield supremacy.

The investment is the latest in a series of broader steps by the Pentagon to accelerate naval shipbuilding and weapons production, spurred by the war on Iran and other regional conflicts that continue to threaten global oil traffic while highlighting the critical role of maritime power.

Anduril, founded in 2017 by Luckey, is best known for its military autonomous systems, drones ‌‌and software.

The startup has, however, expanded beyond drones into maritime and undersea systems, as well as command-and-control software designed to connect military ‌‌sensors, ‌‌weapons and other systems.

The Maryland facility will manufacture torpedo tubes and larger hull components for the US navy’s upgraded Virginia-class fast attack submarines, which the navy is renovating to carry up to 40 Tomahawk missiles each.

While nuclear-powered, the warships are not part of the US’s strategic nuclear deterrent system.

The facility is expected to generate 3,100 jobs while supporting over 11,000 indirect roles.

The navy currently operates 26 Virginia-class fast-attack boats, with two more slated for delivery in 2027. According to reports released by the Department of Defense and navy officials, American shipyards have been struggling to meet the Pentagon’s target production rate of two new boats per year due to persistent supply chain disruptions and labour shortages.

Official disclosures confirm the delivery rate has stalled at just 1.1 to 1.2 submarines annually.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Anduril President Chris Brose said the “main focus” of the new yard was prioritising component manufacturing for the Virginia-class submarines rather than developing any new drone platforms.

“It’s really the government buying the results of what we’re able to produce from the facility ⁠⁠that we’ve invested in,” he said.

articles.title: Flydubai flight incident: Cockpit attack left Captain Smit Machchhar with 'depressed skull fracture'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Captain Smit Machchhar's heroic act of saving flydubai FZ1073 has acquired another dimension with the extent of the injuries he was fighting to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Captain Smit Machchhar's heroic act of saving flydubai FZ1073 has acquired another dimension with the extent of the injuries he was fighting to save the plane from its suicidal Omani co-pilot now coming out.Sources say co-pilot Hammam al-Hammami hitting him with the axe kept in the cockpit had led to a "depressed fracture fragment of skull". An emergency surgery is learnt to have been performed in Saudi Arabia before Captain Machchhar could be flown back to the UAE for further treatment.Dr (Air Cmde) Krishan Kumar Yadav, senior clinical director and professor of neurosurgery and neuro-spine surgery at Marengo Asia Hospitals, told TOI: "A depressed skull fracture is serious. Put simply, a piece of the skull has been pressed inward toward the brain. During surgery, doctors make a careful incision, lift or remove the pressed-in fragment, and check the protective membrane around the brain for tears. They clean the area, repair any damage, and then either replace the bone or reconstruct it. It is delicate work, but it is work we are trained for, and many patients do very well afterwards."The Indian embassy in the UAE said on X Tuesday: "Capt Smit continues to make steady progress and is regaining his health. The embassy remains in close touch with his family, doctors and local authorities, extending all possible assistance. We thank everyone for their prayers & wish him a speedy recovery.""Recovery is not a straight line. The first days are quiet ones: rest, careful monitoring, and keeping him comfortable. Then, bit by bit, strength returns. There will be good days and slower ones. Headaches, tiredness, or trouble concentrating are common while the body heals, and they don't mean something is wrong," Dr Yadav said.Captain Machchhar had told Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu: "It was a normal flight, and the co-pilot wanted to pray, which a lot of locals do. While he was praying, out of respect, I just looked at the front and not at the back." He said that about four or five minutes later, he suddenly felt a heavy blow to the back of his head, which he initially thought was an impact involving the aircraft."After about four or five minutes, my first thought was damage to the aircraft and something is not right. But then the blow kept coming, one after the other. And that's when I realised that it's not the aircraft, it's the other guy who was in the cockpit with me."He tried to stop the co-pilot but was badly affected by the initial blows. "I did try to stop him, but because of his initial blows, my vision was almost like nothing. And I was completely blurred out," the captain said. He then realised the aircraft was descending sharply.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Was Scottish film Till the Bell Rings the first ever 'talkie'?
articles.summary: In 1927, The Jazz Singer made movie history with the first recorded dialogue on film - but new evidence suggests the first feature talking film was Scottish.
articles.body:
"Wait a minute. You ain't heard nothing yet."

That promise, spoken by Al Jolson in the 1927 film The Jazz Singer, made movie history.

The first recorded dialogue on film, Jolson's eight well-chosen words marked the birth of the "talkies", delivered by one of the biggest stars on Earth.

The moment has long been celebrated in popular culture - most memorably in the 1952 film Singin' in the Rain - and there are plans for a variety of events to mark the centenary next year.

But what if those words weren't the first?

Researcher Marc David Jacobs has uncovered evidence that the first-ever talking feature film was Scottish.

And it was screened in Edinburgh - a whole year before Jolson's voice hit the cinemas.

Graham Moffat was a Glaswegian playwright who wrote plays for his touring company. In 1925 he decided to turn his debut play, Till the Bells Ring, into a film.

He approached a London-based company called De Forest Phonofilm, which had patented a system which allowed synchronised audio to be recorded directly onto film.

The early quality was poor, and it was mostly used to record short performances such as vaudeville or music hall acts.

But the Moffats had a much more ambitious plan in mind.

They wanted the entire company involved in a 45-minute feature film with synchronised sound and dialogue throughout.

The cast of six included his wife Margaret - a noted actress and one of the first suffragettes to be arrested in Scotland - and his daughter, Winnifred Moffat.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

A year later, they screened the film, first at a disastrous private demonstration which was marred by faulty equipment.

And then on 11 October in Poole's Synod Hall in Edinburgh, where it was billed as "a super talking picture of Victorian Scottish life".

Jacobs said: "Silent movie audiences would have been used to walking in and out, or leaving halfway through so people had to be warned not to come in in the middle of the film and disturb everyone.

"They had to be told not to talk themselves, just as if they were at an actual play.

"You can see in the reviews, even the sort of people who are professionally being paid to watch these films, there's a sense of wonder."

The film ran for a week, with the Scotsman reporting "the movement and sound are perfectly synchronised and after the listener becomes accustomed to the phenomenon of screen figures appearing to talk and the ear attunes itself to the sounds there is no difficulty in catching the spoken words."

The paper also commended Graham Moffat's "true Scottish humour" and was so impressed with the offering it sent a reporter back for a second screening.

The film was clearly well-marketed and caught the attention of the press.

So why has it fallen into obscurity in the history of sound on film?

According to Jacobs, the film was acquired by an unscrupulous exhibitor who re-released it in 1933 as a brand-new film.

Moffat sued and won his case in 1935, after which all copies of the feature were returned to him. But the film was apparently never shown again.

He died in Cape Town in December 1951, never having made another.

One of his plays - Bunty Pulls the Strings - became a huge hit on Broadway, but his landmark contribution to cinema has never been recognised or celebrated.

And the film itself? Jacobs believes the only surviving copy of Till the Bells Ring is in the BFI National Archive in Hertfordshire.

It has not been shown privately or publicly since being acquired by the BFI more than 50 years ago.

He hopes the print can be examined and restored and a search undertaken for any other surviving material.

And he feels that would see the Moffats and their film get the credit they are due.

"I was amazed to discover the unbelievable story of the Scottish family production that beat Hollywood to the punch," he said.

"But I was even more astonished by the complete lack of interest in it.

"It was as if it was impossible to believe that a major piece of world cinema could have come out of a tiny London studio, hired by a canny Glaswegian playwright.

"But it did. And nearly a century after it was last seen, the time has finally come for the world to recognise Graham and Maggie Moffat's world-beating achievement."

And the first words ever spoken in the world's first talking feature?

The heroine, Aggie, says: "Still anither mornin' and never a word or a sign o' him. Eh, me! The sun's gettin' through, so we'll be wearin' oor braws to the kirk the day."

To be fair, Al probably had the better line.

articles.title: Powys farmer says abuse from dad was 'torture'
articles.summary: Tracy Lewis loved growing up on a farm but said the abuse from her father was terrifying.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains content that some readers might find distressing

Growing up on a farm, Tracy Lewis loved being around their animals but said the physical and emotional abuse from her farmer father was "torture".

When she was eight, she recalled her dad pulling her out of bed by her hair to go lambing as her battered mum told her "you have to get the lamb out or we're both going to die".

Tracy, now 48 and a farmer herself, and other domestic abuse survivors are calling on governments to better support victims in rural areas.

The UK government said it was working to address disparities while the Welsh government said challenges will be considered in its next national strategy.

For many people the idea of growing up in the mid Wales countryside surrounded by trees and animals sounds idyllic, but Tracy says her dad was physically and emotionally abusive.

Tracy's family have given their permission to the BBC for her to share her story.

"I remember my father pulled me out of bed by my hair to go and lamb a ewe," she recalled.

"I walked past the bathroom and my mum's face had blood all over it and her nose was squashed, she'd been crying. She said to me, you have to get the lamb out or we're both going to die."

Tracy said the animals would sometimes be used as a form of control or a catalyst for abuse.

"I was getting beaten up when something died, my mum was getting hurt when an animal was poorly," she recalled. "It felt like slavery, we loved the animals and farming but we were isolated and stuck."

Tracy, who was raised at the farm in Llanbister in Powys, would sometimes think about calling Childline as she said she felt so petrified.

"The farming world is the best place to be, neighbours will always help you out but abuse can be hidden very easily," said the mum-of-three.

"Everyone knows everybody, but what goes on behind closed doors will stay behind closed doors.

"For me it was terror and horror, my mum got the worst of it and she tried her best to protect us. But she was totally isolated, the farm was her life."

She said farmers often had generational businesses and relied on markets and trade with others, adding that raising abuse could affect livelihoods.

Tracy also claims her father, who is now dead, financially abused her, stating that the farm would be passed down to her.

She said she worked on it for 20 years and paid rent to him under the impression the family farm would one day become hers.

After finding out it was not left to her in his will, she said she has had to "fight" to retain ownership of it.

Tracy is one of about 11 million people living in rural areas - more than 15% of the UK population.

The National Rural Crime Network says the true picture of rural abuse is often hidden, with survivors often having more barriers to reach support.

One smallholding owner said her rurality enabled an ex-partner to hold her at gunpoint for eight hours with no-one to hear her screams.

Rhianon Bragg said she screamed when Gareth Wyn Jones ambushed her with the gun in north Wales in 2019 but knew that no-one would hear her because she lives rurally.

"There were several moments that night when I thought I wouldn't see my children again," she recalled.

Rhianon has spoken in-depth about her experience at her smallholding in Gwynedd as part of a new BBC iPlayer series It Happened To Me .

She has since worked with agencies like the police to try to address issues about domestic abuse and stalking in rural areas.

"Domestic abuse changed our home from a place of peaceful seclusion to a place of vulnerable isolation and what I experienced was the additional barriers that living rurally created," said Rhianon.

She said all UK and Welsh government domestic abuse policies should be "rural proofed" and highlighted issues such as internet connectivity and distance from police stations.

"There is so much that should be addressed for people to be treated evenly, and at the moment, if you live rurally you're on the back foot," said Rhianon.

Tracy urged anyone affected by abuse to speak out about it.

"Tell someone, a friend, a neighbour, once you start telling people, things will move," she said.

"A good overhaul of policy would be for the best because out here you can hide a lot of stuff. I think there's a lot more domestic violence that goes on in rural communities than anyone will ever know," added Tracy.

A report by the UK's first working group focused on rural inequality and domestic abuse said rural domestic abuse victims were being failed.

As part of a 12-point plan, the report published in May by RiTA - Rural Initiatives Tackling Abuse - recommended the UK government establish a parliamentary commission on rural domestic abuse and "rural-proof" government strategies.

The Domestic Abuse Commissioner for England and Wales said she "welcomed" the report and told the BBC the realities of rural life for victims can be "frequently weaponised by their perpetrators".

Dame Nicole Jacobs said: "If we're serious about tackling domestic abuse and addressing inequalities across society, services and support must be designed with rural victims in mind.

"That means making sure rural communities are not overlooked and ensuring specialist services have the funding and resources they need to reach every victim, wherever they live."

The report follows a 2019 National Rural Crime Network's Captive and Controlled report which suggested domestic abuse lasts 25% longer on average in the most rural areas compared with towns and cities.

"In rural Wales, distance is not just geography - it has a real impact on whether someone can access safety and support," said Hayley Heard, of Montgomeryshire Family Crisis Centre.

"Domestic abuse thrives on isolation," added Hayley. "In a rural community, that isolation can be magnified.

"There may be no transport, nowhere private to go and sometimes a fear that everyone will know if you ask for help."

The centre said they supported 296 women, 88 men and 231 children in the last financial year and feel "there is a huge gap between rural and urban domestic abuse".

Hayley said covering a rural part of the country like north Powys - an area of 839sq miles (2,173sq km) and which can take four hours to travel from one end to the other - came with extra costs such as fuel to cover long distances.

The charity recently lost a funding bid for around £102,000 and as chief executive, Hayley said the impact was "quite catastrophic".

"That was to maintain our children's and young persons project who do a lot of work within schools," she said.

"Raising awareness needs to be something we need to promote. The abuse isn't different living rurally but the barriers are different."

Tracy said that school was a "saviour" for her as a child and that the money would have been "invaluable".

"If we can explain to children what abuse is and what it looks like, that would be a really good place to start," she added.

The UK government said they were "working to address disparities in provision" and have pledged more than £1bn in dedicated funding over the next three years to improve support to rural victims.

"Close collaboration with charities and community organisations is helping us better understand the barriers facing rural communities," they said in a statement.

"No victim of domestic abuse should be denied support because of where they live."

More than three-quarters of Wales is rural, and the Welsh government said they "recognised victims and survivors in rural communities can face more barriers to accessing help".

"These challenges will be considered in our next national strategy to help ensure services are able to meet the needs of people across all parts of Wales," they added.

"No-one should ever be made to feel unsafe, scared, or at risk of abuse in their homes and communities."

If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line .

articles.title: This Canadian couple bought a retired school bus for $7,200; after a year and $30,000 in renovations, it became a full-sized home with a king bedroom, kitchen, bathroom and solar power
articles.summary: A retired school bus is not an obvious starting point for a home, but for Tanya Nestoruk and Arya Touserkani it offered something their previous house and
articles.body: A retired school bus is not an obvious starting point for a home, but for Tanya Nestoruk and Arya Touserkani it offered something their previous house and first van could not. The Canadian couple wanted to travel while keeping their living space with them, and a second-hand bus gave them enough room to build a more permanent setup. They removed its original fittings, added a bedroom, kitchen and bathroom, installed solar panels and created storage throughout the interior. The project took far longer than the six months they had initially planned, but by the time they left for Mexico, the former school vehicle had become a compact home capable of supporting life on the road.Couple turns an old school bus into a home built for travellingNestoruk and Touserkani had been living in a four-bedroom house in Canada when they decided in 2021 to change direction. They sold the property and moved into a van, hoping that a smaller home would make it easier to travel and spend more time outdoors.In an interview with CNBC Make It, Nestoruk said, “I love the simplicity and versatility of being able to live and travel wherever you want, have minimal impact, and explore new places.”The arrangement worked for a while. After several months, though, they realised that they wanted more space. A school bus seemed to offer a middle ground: it could still move from place to place, but its larger interior allowed them to create something closer to a conventional home.For Nestoruk, who works as an environmental educator, there was also an appeal in giving an old vehicle another purpose. Touserkani is a photographer, and the couple were interested in a lifestyle that allowed them to keep travelling without giving up the basic comforts of a home. They eventually found a retired school bus through Facebook Marketplace.A $7,200 bus becomes a demanding DIY projectThe seller was a school bus contractor, which turned out to be useful. The vehicle came with maintenance records and, according to the couple, had been reasonably well looked after. Its final school run was followed almost immediately by a very different journey. Nestoruk and Touserkani bought the bus for $7,200, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It, then took it home and began planning the conversion.They had originally hoped to complete the renovation in six months. The reality was considerably more demanding.The couple wanted to do much of the work themselves, so their days were spent constructing parts of the interior and their evenings researching how to tackle whatever came next. Touserkani described becoming deeply absorbed in the project, with YouTube videos and online searches becoming part of the daily routine.Inside the bus, a full-sized home takes shapeThe renovation was not simply a matter of stripping the vehicle and replacing everything with new materials. The couple looked for ways to give some of the bus's original components another use. The old seats were donated to a local children's camp, while the luggage racks were sold to someone who planned to repurpose them in a garage. It was one way of reducing what would otherwise have been discarded during the conversion.Inside, the layout gradually took shape around the couple's needs. There is a bedroom large enough for a king-sized bed, a living area with a custom pull-out sofa, a kitchen and a bathroom.The kitchen includes a three-burner hob and oven. They also found an RV washer and dryer through Facebook Marketplace, adding another domestic feature that would have been difficult to fit into their earlier van. The couple spent about $30,000 on the renovation and around a year turning the bus into a functioning home.The couple redesigned the bus around everyday practicalitySome of the bus's most distinctive features were added for practical reasons rather than appearance. Touserkani is 6ft 1in, which made the original interior height particularly awkward. Two skylights helped solve that problem. They allowed the couple to raise the roof in specific areas rather than undertaking a much larger and more expensive roof modification across the whole vehicle. The openings also brought considerably more daylight into the interior.Storage was built into different parts of the bus, including concealed spaces for food and belongings. An on-demand water heater was installed as part of the system. The result is less like the inside of a conventional coach and more like a compact flat that happens to have wheels.The couple added outdoor features for travel and everyday livingSolar panels were installed so the couple could live without relying entirely on conventional electrical connections. That fitted with their broader aim of keeping their environmental footprint as low as they could while travelling.Their approach also extended to the outside of the bus. They built a set of stairs leading to the roof and added a rear hitch deck, welded by a friend, for carrying their motorcycles. The bikes became their everyday transport when the bus itself stayed parked.There is also an outdoor table, which gives them somewhere to eat or barbecue and provides an additional space for visitors.Mexico became the next destinationThe original six-month renovation deadline was partly driven by the couple's plans to leave Canada before winter. They wanted to follow warmer weather and head towards Baja California in Mexico. They eventually stopped working on the bus in November 2022 and set off.The vehicle has since made the journey between Canada and Mexico several times. For the couple, the bus became more than simply somewhere to sleep between trips. It allowed them to take their home with them while moving between places.You use AI every day. articles.title: Transgender Washington state resident accused of fueling deadly Canadian school massacre that killed 8: DOJ
articles.summary: James Cody Bryant allegedly sent money, offered advice and agreed to livestream the Tumbler Ridge school shooting instead of alerting law enforcement.
articles.body: A transgender Washington state resident allegedly helped fuel a Canadian school massacre that left children dead, choosing to aid the shooter, who also identified as a transgender, instead of sounding the alarm, federal officials said Tuesday. James Cody Bryant, 30, was arrested Tuesday morning in Bellingham north of Seattle, accused of sending money, offering advice and agreeing to broadcast the Feb. 10 attack at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School in British Columbia. "Bryant had the information and ability to alert law enforcement, and even discussed that possibility with the shooter, but he chose not to," Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd said at a Seattle news conference. "Instead, he encouraged and offered assistance to a murderer." TRANSGEDNER EX-STUDENT IDENTIFIED AS ALLEGED SUSPECT IN DEADLY CANADA SCHOOL MASS SHOOTING Bryant faces a federal charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country. Prosecutors allege Bryant helped the shooter, 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, start a car to reach the school after the killings had begun. "So even after the shooter had already tragically killed two family members, Bryant assisted the shooter in successfully traveling to the second location to take even more lives," FBI Seattle Special Agent in Charge W. Mike Herrington said. "In the complaint, Bryant even admits to being maybe the only one who could stop the shooter." Herrington confirmed that Bryant and Van Rootselaar both identified as transgender, and said Bryant identifies as female. The two met through a random pairing on the online chat service Omegle roughly three years before the attack. Investigators have no indication what their transgender identities were, why they remained in contact, or that they ever met in person, Herrington said. TEEN PLANNED MIDDLE SCHOOL MASSACRE BEFORE MAKING DEADLY ‘LAST-MINUTE CHOICE’ TO KILL MOM: OFFICIAL Their online friendship developed into discussions of violence over at least six months, according to Herrington. "This complaint was particularly difficult to read, in part because of the casual tone these two individuals used when discussing the mass taking of innocent lives that was being planned," he said. Bryant allegedly agreed to record and broadcast a livestream to maximize the shooter’s notoriety. "Bryant even stayed awake after an overnight work shift to make sure this horrific act could be widely viewed online," Herrington said. FLORIDA MAN INDICTED FOR ALLEGEDLY PLOTTING MASS SHOOTING TARGETING JEWISH EMPLOYEES AT ADVOCACY ORGANIZATION "We certainly know the shooter was concerned that not enough people would see the livestream without Bryant broadcasting it, and was depending on Bryant to amplify the livestream because the shooter did not have many followers on social media." Floyd said the attempted livestream on Twitch lasted about 20 seconds before shutting down. Herrington said investigators do not know whether Van Rootselaar would have carried out the attack without Bryant’s willingness to operate it. Officials also described financial assistance, including a little more than $100 for shoes. An attempted transfer of roughly $15 for a lighter was ultimately reversed. NAVY VETERAN AMONG TRIO WHO ALLEGEDLY WANTED TO BEHEAD SOLDIER AND FUND ISIS DRONE ATTACKS ON AMERICANS Floyd said Bryant and the shooter discussed sending weapons to Canada, but Bryant was uncomfortable doing so. Herrington said investigators had no indication the guns used in the attack came from the U.S. Asked about a possible political ideology or group affiliation, Floyd said investigators had no information indicating either. Herrington pointed to the shooter’s suffering and "a very keen focus on notoriety" as themes in the communications. The pair discussed other mass shootings, how the public reacted and a desire for the Tumbler Ridge attack to receive similar attention, he said. The investigation crossed the border within days of the massacre, when Canadian police received information from an online platform used by the shooter and contacted the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), British Columbia RCMP Assistant Commissioner Elija Rain said. Floyd said investigators obtained subpoenas and warrants and reviewed thousands of communications, many on Discord, before making the arrest. Canadian investigators have reviewed more than 90 statements from students, educators and first responders and continue to examine other online contacts, Rain said. GEORGIA HIGH SCHOOL SHOOTING SUSPECT COLT GRAY CHANGES PLEA TO GUILTY, NOW FACES LIFE IN PRISON "Our RCMP criminal investigation remains ongoing and the possibility of further charges being pursued in Canada remains under active consideration," he said. Herrington warned that assisting a mass shooting from afar does not shield someone from prosecution. "If you think you are safe from prosecution because you did not pull the trigger, or were not physically present at the scene of the crime, think again," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The FBI and our partners will use all of the considerable investigative tools at our disposal to hold accountable those who enable or assist in acts of mass violence." The Feb. 10 attack killed eight victims, including five students, an educator and the shooter’s mother and 11-year-old stepbrother, according to Canadian authorities. Van Rootselaar was found dead inside the school from an apparent self-inflicted injury.

articles.title: Sally Yates, former acting AG who clashed with Trump, leading Cornell assault probe
articles.summary: The longtime federal prosecutor became known for refusing to enforce Trump’s ban on travelers to the U.S. from predominantly Muslim countries.
articles.body: Sally Yates, whose career in the Justice Department spanned about three decades, will lead an independent review on how Cornell University responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus, the university announced Tuesday. The decision comes in the wake of national outrage over a former Cornell student’s allegation last month that she was gang-raped and plied with drugs at a fraternity in 2024. New York Attorney General Letitia James is also investigating the allegation. A spokesperson said staff members from the attorney general’s office have “spoken with the Tompkins County District Attorney, Jane Doe’s attorney, and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation.” The independent probe headed by Yates will look into how the university responded to those allegations and whether the school followed its policies and procedures, according to the university. More broadly, the review will examine Cornell’s policies and practices spanning from prevention to response. It will include how reports are investigated, how disciplinary decisions are handled and how students are supported, the university said. The investigation will also look into the role and response of campus police, and its coordination with other law enforcement agencies and prosecutors. Yates did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “Sally Yates brings extraordinary experience, independence and judgment to this work,” Anne Meinig Smalling, the chair of the university’s Special Committee of the Cornell University Board of Trustees, said in a statement. An attorney for one of the Chi Phi members who was accused of sexual assault, Gillio Lopes, said they welcome the independent investigation. “Sally Yates has tremendous experience as a prosecutor and investigator, and she and her team should have access to the full record and the freedom to follow the facts wherever they lead,” attorney Andrew Miltenberg said. Lopes denies sexually assaulting the former student and disagreed with the Title IX finding, he said. Attorneys for several of the other men have denied wrongdoing or disputed Doe’s account. Yates is a longtime federal prosecutor who became known in 2017 for refusing to enforce President Donald Trump’s ban on travelers to the U.S. from predominantly Muslim countries. Currently a partner at the law firm King & Spalding, she also previously investigated allegations of abuse and misconduct at U.S. Soccer. Yates was named the deputy U.S. attorney general, the second-highest-ranking in the Justice Department, with bipartisan support in 2015. During that tenure under former President Barack Obama, Yates wrote a memo directing prosecutors to focus on individual wrongdoers in corporate cases. The memo followed the fallout of the 2008 financial crisis, in which corporations were forced to pay fines but many individual executives were not prosecuted. Yates was also the acting U.S. attorney general for 10 days in 2017 before she was fired for refusing to defend Trump’s travel ban. Trump’s order created an early flashpoint of protest against his aggressive immigration policies. The White House said at the time that Yates had “betrayed the Department of Justice by refusing to enforce a legal order designed to protect the citizens of the United States.” The statement added that “Ms. Yates is an Obama Administration appointee who is weak on borders and very weak on illegal immigration.” Yates wrote an op-ed in The New York Times in July 2017, after her firing, writing that Trump was “attempting to dismantle the rule of law, destroy the time-honored independence of the Justice Department, and undermine the career men and women who are devoted to seeking justice day in and day out, regardless of which political party is in power.” “If we are not careful, when we wake up from the Trump presidency, our justice system may be broken beyond recognition,” she wrote. Yates began her career in the DOJ in 1989 at the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia, where she was an assistant U.S. attorney. That office covers 46 counties and includes Atlanta. In 2010, Obama appointed her to lead the office, making her the first woman to do so. She has also previously led investigations into sexual misconduct. In 2022, Yates led an independent probe into U.S. Soccer that resulted in a damning report. “Our investigation over the past year has revealed a league in which abuse was systematic. Verbal and emotional abuse and sexual misconduct occurred at multiple teams, was perpetrated by several coaches and affected many players,” she said at the time. U.S. Soccer said that the findings were “heartbreaking and deeply troubling” and that it would work to thoroughly address the recommendations. “The abuse described is inexcusable and has no place on any playing field, in any training facility or workplace,” U.S. Soccer President and former U.S. Women’s National Team member Cindy Parlow Cone said at the time. In Cornell’s announcement on Monday, it said that Yates and her team have been asked to “examine Cornell’s overall approach to preventing and responding to sexual misconduct, identify where we are doing things well and where we can do better, and recommend changes that will help make our community safer.” The university said it would share the results of the review, along with any recommendations, with the Cornell community.

articles.title: US reups do-not-travel warning for Russia over ‘suspected pneumonic plague’
articles.summary: The U.S. is refreshing its call for Americans not to travel to Russia in the wake of a suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia. In a post on the social platform X on Tuesday, the State Department said, “The U.S. Embassy is aware of press reports from the Irkutsk region of suspected pneumonic plague…
articles.body:
The U.S. is refreshing its call for Americans not to travel to Russia in the wake of a suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia.

In a post on the social platform X on Tuesday, the State Department said, “The U.S. Embassy is aware of press reports from the Irkutsk region of suspected pneumonic plague resulting in the death of an individual and of associated quarantine measures in, and closures of, hospitals in Irkutsk.”

“We continue to track the situation closely. The U.S. government has limited ability to help U.S. citizens in Russia, especially outside of Moscow,” the department continued. “The State Department’s Level 4 Travel Advisory (Do Not Travel) for Russia remains in place and states U.S. citizens currently in Russia should depart immediately.”

On Monday, President Trump said he was worried about the suspected plague case, saying the U.S. was “looking at it very strongly.”

The State Department also said Monday it was monitoring it.

“I hate to see them having it,” Trump told reporters before departing the White House for Nebraska. “It’s a rough disease. We used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter.”

NBC News reported Monday that around 200 people in Siberia were facing medical observation in the wake of a 28-year-old lab worker, possibly exposed to the pneumonic plague, dying, local media reported.

On Sunday, the Russian consumer welfare service said the woman, who worked at an institute combating the plague, died due to “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” NBC News reported. However, a specific cause of death was not given by Russian authorities.

articles.title: Nepal floods: Many of those swept away aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo
articles.summary: Relatives are finding themselves with no compensation and facing an administrative nightmare.
articles.body:
At the Pashupatinath temple, on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Madan Lal Lawat joined other families in honouring loved ones who were lost when a deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border last month.

In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead, allowing relatives to perform last rites.

With more than 5,000 people still missing and the government ending rescue operations, this is the only way people like Lawat can honour the dead.

Five of his relatives - including his brother - were caught in the water's onslaught and are still missing. Lawat survived because he was driving his bus outside his village, Betrawati.

The last Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave.

"I don't know how to start over. Police say they're still searching for the bodies, but I'm not sure they'll ever be found," Lawat says.

But legally, their fate is far more complicated. In Nepal, a missing person is only presumed dead after 12 years.

Section 40 of Nepal's Civil Code does allow for some exceptions, but it does not have a provision for disasters like the flood witnessed last month.

Families like Lawat's have told the BBC they are struggling to obtain death certificates, affecting everything from accessing flood compensation to the transfer of properties and even inheritance.

Relatives can receive up to 25,000 rupees (£122; $162) for funeral costs, in addition to about 200,000 rupees (£981; $1,302) in bereavement compensation for the first relative who died, and 100,000 rupees (£491; $651) for each additional death.

But this is only possible once they submit a death certificate. So as families try to rebuild their lives, many are now caught in an administrative nightmare.

"In view of the current disaster, the law is outdated," says constitutional law expert, Bipin Adhikari.

He explains the law was meant to account for people who travelled abroad and weren't heard from for years. "But technology has advanced now, it isn't as difficult to send or receive information," he argues.

For Lawat, the legal minefield has made an already devastating loss even harder to navigate.

When he tried to obtain a death certificate last week, officials at the local municipality office turned him away. "They said they're still discussing the death certificate issue. We aren't sure what to do now. There's so much uncertainty," he tells us.

Even when bodies are recovered, identifying their identities is a slow and challenging task. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered so far, and Nepal has little experience in processing DNA at such scale. In some cases, authorities have taken DNA samples, then buried the bodies with markers in the ground, should families claim them.

Given the scale of damage and loss, families say compensation is desperately needed.

Nepal's latest assessment counts 7,570 private buildings damaged or destroyed, home to nearly 33,000 people based on census data.

The BBC visited Lawat's village Betrawati just days after the disaster, once the roads to the district of Rasuwa had been cleared. For days, this area had been cut off from the capital Kathmandu, and struggling with a shortage of basic supplies including petrol.

The damage in the village was staggering. The ground was nothing but hardened mud and silt. Footage of the flood showed it had swallowed most of the village in just minutes. There was no sign of its bustling market, the local Uttargaya School was in ruins, the houses swept away, and school buses were turned over.

Betrawati straddles flood-devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot, and is part of the Bidur municipality, where the government estimates more than 3,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. It's the largest amount of any municipality.

Local governments are now urging the prime minister's office to figure out a way to resolve the death confirmation issue.

"Everything is on hold," Bidur's Mayor, Rajan Shrestha, told the BBC.

He said it could take up to 12 years for relatives to access the funds they are entitled to.

For one of South Asia's smallest economies, finding money for compensation is a challenge, and the sums on offer are small when compared with the scale of the losses.

The government puts damage to personal belongings alone at £123 million ($165 million) across more than 8,300 households.

This implies losses of about £14,800 ($20,000) on average per household, though this figure is only based on census data and modelling, and doesn't represent the exact cost per family.

The financial toll makes the death certificates vital for families trying to recover from the disaster.

Shrestha is calling on the federal government to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Until then, he says his hands are tied.

"We understand the emotional pain for families who have already performed funeral rituals, but officials must work within legal boundaries to avoid future liabilities."

The government has told the BBC it is trying to find a solution.

In a statement, the prime minister's office said it was "aware of the difficulties" the law may cause families in "exceptional circumstances, including disasters". The home ministry said the government was taking the issue seriously and was ready to amend the law, if required.

The legal hurdles families are facing comes as Nepal faces a steep reconstruction bill, which the government says could cost up to £3.6bn ($4.8bn).

At the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Balen Shah explained rebuilding the country would require more than 10% of its gross domestic product, an enormous burden on the country's economy.

Dozens of public buildings including schools, health clinics and hospitals have been wrecked by the floods. That's in addition to roads, bridges, wastewater treatment plants and hydropower projects.

Shah is now pushing for grant-based international support rather than new loans. Nepal is one of the lowest emitters of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet one one of the most vulnerable countries to global warming.

"When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan or a patchwork of small grants," he told a room full of world leaders.

This is not the first time Nepal has had to recover after a devastating natural disaster.

For Tisum Ghale, the past month has been painfully familiar.

He and his family lost their home in an earthquake in 2015, and became displaced for months. They eventually settled in Betrawati.

But the place that was once a refuge is where 19 of his relatives were killed in last month's flood, including five of his sisters. He survived because he was doing construction work outside of the village.

So far he has received no compensation. He desperately needs the money after his home was washed away and he looks after eight children left behind by his sisters. He is one of the thousands displaced, living across 37 holding centres in northern Nepal.

Like Lawati and thousands of other families, Ghale plans on holding a funeral without his loved ones' bodies.

He hopes the law will eventually recognise what he already knows: his loved ones will not be coming home.

articles.title: Costco rolls out new Disneyland ticket deal but there's a catch for parkgoers
articles.summary: Costco's $329.99 Disneyland bundle includes a two-day Park Hopper ticket, Lightning Lane Multi Pass and a $60 dining card at select California stores.
articles.body: Disneyland visitors have a new ticket option that bundles park admission with other perks — but there are some restrictions that travelers may want to know about. Costco is offering a two-day Disneyland Resort Park Hopper ticket with Lightning Lane Multi Pass and a $60 dining card for $329.99 at select locations in California. Disneyland Resort officials confirmed the offer to Fox News Digital, saying it rolled out last week at select Costco stores across the state. DISNEYLAND CRACKS DOWN ON GUESTS WITH SWEEPING NEW RESTRICTIONS, SPARKING BACKLASH The resort regularly makes limited-time ticket offers available throughout the year, including through third-party retailers, according to Disneyland Resort officials. The Costco package has since caught the attention of theme park fans online as travelers compare the price with the cost of purchasing tickets directly from Disneyland. In a recent Instagram post, one theme park content creator highlighted the $329.99 price and the included Lightning Lane access and dining card. "Costco has a Disneyland deal right now that is actually WORTH talking about!" the user wrote. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER By comparison, a two-day Park Hopper ticket is currently listed at $445 for one adult on Disneyland's website, before adding Lightning Lane — though pricing is subject to change. That puts the Costco package about $115 below the currently listed two-day Park Hopper price, although the two options come with different terms and restrictions. The offer also comes as Disneyland adjusted some of its ticket prices this week. Mid-tier single-day tickets increased by $5, while the least expensive $104 ticket and the highest-priced $224 ticket remained unchanged, according to the Los Angeles Times. The cost of Lightning Lane can now reach $38, up $1, while the Park Hopper add-on for single-day tickets increased by $5 to $10, depending on the date, the outlet reported. Multi-day ticket prices were unchanged. Hugh Johnston, CFO of The Walt Disney Company, speaking at the recent Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference in San Francisco, said the company is keeping ticket prices accessible for younger families by offering lower rates during off-peak value periods. "It's something that we're acutely sensitive to because we want to make sure we continue to bring young families, in particular, into the parks and develop that Disney love, right?" he said. "So we're super sensitive to the fact that, particularly in the value times of the year, we keep those ticket prices relatively low so that we can actually encourage those young families to come in," he added. "We want to make sure we continue to bring young families, in particular, into the parks." The Costco ticket can be used between Oct. 2 and Dec. 18, according to information shared by the Instagram user. Once a guest uses the ticket for the first time, the second park day must be used within 13 days, the video said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Theme park reservations are also required for each visit, and the ticket is nonrefundable, according to the information shared online. The same person must use both days of the ticket, meaning the two visits cannot be split between different travelers. The offer is currently limited to select Costco locations in California, Disneyland Resort officials told Fox News Digital. The package has generated mixed reactions among Disney fans online, with some questioning the cost of park visits and others praising the bundled price. articles.title: US tries new Sudan strategy as war fueled by ‘external actors’ drags on
articles.summary: The Trump administration is signaling a change in course on Sudan, facing months of failed diplomacy to achieve a ceasefire in the more than three-year conflict, a fight largely between two main warring factions but supported by a constellation of international backers. The U.S. is pushing at the United Nations Security Council a proposal to…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is signaling a change in course on Sudan, facing months of failed diplomacy to achieve a ceasefire in the more than three-year conflict, a fight largely between two main warring factions but supported by a constellation of international backers.

The U.S. is pushing at the United Nations Security Council a proposal to expand an arms embargo to the whole country, broadening it well beyond its current single region. The plan comes up for a vote Thursday.

The U.S. proposal proved polarizing, and divisions came to a head in September, when the Security Council only managed to extend the arms embargo on Sudan’s western Darfur region — a 21-year-old measure called Resolution 1591 — for one month, until Oct. 9. It was the shortest extension ever issued for 1591.

“The entire country is awash with weapons. Our position is that neither side needs additional weapons,” Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told Foreign Policy late last month.

The Trump administration argues that expanding the arms embargo to the whole country allows for the U.N. to take a fuller picture of violations and networks moving weapons and to document who flouts the embargo.

The proposal has put the U.S., United Kingdom and their backers on one side, and China, Russia and their backers on the other. It’s not clear if opposition among the veto-wielding permanent members could tank 1591 in its entirety.

While Resolution 1591 has failed to stem weapons flows into the country, it is useful for its Panel of Experts, which monitors and reports on violations while recommending people and entities for sanctions.

The U.S. proposal would add new pressure on Sudan’s Armed Forces (SAF), which is fighting the breakaway paramilitary group the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), by expanding the reporting requirements in 1591. The most recent report provided details on how the territory of the United Arab Emirates is a key link in arms transfers to the RSF — which Abu Dhabi rejects — but that investigations into the SAF’s procurement network, particularly drones, are “preliminary.”

Expanding 1591 gained the backing of a group of Senate Democrats, who wrote a letter to the administration to urge that reporting requirements include “explicit documentation of all violations of the arms embargo and the parties responsible.”

“Countries who blatantly circumvent the arms embargo and other UN restrictions to prolong the conflict cannot be permitted to continue hiding their role and must be publicly held to account for their actions,” they wrote.

Although it’s not a secret who is backing the main warring parties in Sudan’s war.

Saudi Arabia and Egypt lead a larger coalition supporting SAF Gen. Abdel-Fattah al-Burhan, while the United Arab Emirates is the main backer of Burhan’s former deputy, Gen. Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo, as head of the paramilitary group the RSF.

Those three countries, along with the U.S., are part of a “Quad” group that proposed a ceasefire in September 2025 that has failed to take root. A renewed push in July for a 90-day truce stalled in the face of SAF demands that the RSF withdraw from cities it has occupied since May 2023.

“Every time it seems like we’re on the verge of making progress, one side or the other will back off because they think they’re winning or they think they could win,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in September.

Sudan’s war is the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. At least 150,000 people are believed to have been killed , with some killing campaigns amounting to genocide, according to U.N. monitors and a U.S. determination.

More than 33 million people require assistance and 9 million people are displaced inside the country, with more than 4 million refugees and “irregular arrivals” to Europe increasing . The United Nations’s appeal for nearly $3 billion in humanitarian aid for Sudan is only 43 percent funded .

The SAF has gained some battlefield momentum. The army-appointed prime minister declared victory in the war over a year into retaking the capital, Khartoum, during a visit by The Hill in April .

Sudanese Armed Forces made further significant territorial gains over the summer, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED). But an escalating air and drone warfare campaign is having an outsize impact on civilian casualties, with 1,000 people killed in drone attacks in the first half of 2026.

The SAF and countries backing it say the U.S. push for a country-wide arms embargo unfairly draws equivalency between the SAF and RSF. Both sides are accused of carrying out war crimes, but the RSF’s siege on the city of El Fasher was determined a genocide by the former Biden administration.

“The council must preserve the distinction between the national armed forces of a sovereign state and a militia accused of mass atrocities and genocidal violence,” Pakistan’s ambassador to the United Nations, Asim Iftikhar Ahmad, said during a Security Council meeting in August. Pakistan is one of the 10 nonpermanent members that will vote Thursday on whether to expand 1591.

The SAF and its backers further took exception when the U.S. reportedly conditioned a visa for Burhan to attend the U.N. General Assembly in September in exchange for accepting the ceasefire, according to Reuters.

The Saudis reportedly threatened to exit the Quad over the Burhan snub, according to The Africa Report.

In an apparent effort to smooth relations, Massad Boulos, Trump’s point person on Sudan and father-in-law to the president’s daughter, highlighted that he was in the same meeting space as Burhan during a luncheon in Egypt on Sunday.

A Sudanese government official told The Hill that no meeting took place and that Burhan did not exchange any words with Boulos.

Taken together, the U.S. is signaling increased pressure on the SAF, said Areig Elhag, Arabic content editor at The Washington Institute for Near East Policy, signaling a strategy focusing on who can legitimately govern Sudan in its next phase.

“The RSF already has very limited political legitimacy inside Sudan, but the SAF has continued to represent Sudan in many international and regional institutions,” she said.

“So the U.S. position is significant because it is also moving away from the idea that the SAF should automatically be treated as the legitimate political authority. So the pressure is mainly on SAF.”

Burhan seized his authority as president of the country’s Transitional Sovereignty Council in a 2021 coup, which initially included the RSF’s Hemeditti. At that time, the civilian head of the transitional government was Prime Minister Abdallah Hamdok.

Hamdok, in an interview last week with Al Monitor during a visit to Washington, D.C., said the Trump administration appears to be applying greater pressure on the SAF and RSF, shifting from what he described as a “soft” approach.

“I do not think these generals respond to niceties,” Hamdok told the outlet . “They need to be told bluntly that there are consequences to what they are doing.”

But the U.S. is still holding back public pressure on the war’s international backers. Rubio, during his appearance at the UN in September, said naming and shaming those countries would contribute to “friction.”

“There are external actors. I’m not going to single them out. You know who they are. I don’t want to create any more friction than there needs to be created,” he said.

“But that war and that conflict and that crisis would not be happening were it not for the active participation of external actors that are feeding one side of that conflict or another.”

The refusal to call out the countries enabling Sudan’s war is only one of the many confusions and contradictions of the Trump administration’s policy toward Sudan and overlapping crises in the Horn of Africa, said Michelle Gavin, senior fellow for Africa policy studies with the Council on Foreign Relations, said of the U.S. proposal.

“There’s something a bit through the looking glass about these repeated Quad statements about the need for external actors stopping their support for the war , signed by the external actors supporting the war,” she said.

“It really, to me, looks like a total unwillingness to take on very, very deep-pocketed potential partners in some of this, the deal making, that seems to be part and parcel of U.S. foreign policy these days.”

articles.title: ‘We are desperate’: Venezuela’s power cuts fuel growing public anger
articles.summary: Frequent outages have fuelled protests against the government of interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez.
articles.body:
The hum of the kidney dialysis machine that Onasis Munoz is connected to suddenly stops. The fluorescent lights overhead flicker out, and his room at a clinic in Valencia, Venezuela, is plunged into darkness.

It is not the first time a power cut has interrupted one of the three weekly sessions Munoz needs to do the work his failing kidneys can no longer do, filtering waste and excess fluid from his blood.

For years, electricity would go out every couple of days across parts of Venezuela's Carabobo state.

But in recent months, Munoz said, the outages have grown to be daily, lasting around seven hours. The clinic's emergency batteries have since been depleted, and its backup generator no longer works.

He explained that the frequent power failures have disrupted his treatment. His health has slumped as a result.

"I arrive home, exhausted, as if I had run a marathon," the 34-year-old said.

But often there is no electricity there either, and recent weeks have been sweltering. "I can't switch on the air conditioning. I cannot rest because of the heat and the mosquitoes. There's no relief," Munoz said.

Across Venezuela, the prolonged outages are riling locals, as the electricity supply to homes, businesses and essential services becomes unstable.

Some of the cuts are deliberate, as the government of interim President Delcy Rodriguez rations electricity.

The resulting frustration has spilled onto the streets, where demonstrators hold "cacerolazos" – a traditional form of protest that involves banging pots and pans.

Some have gone as far as blocking roadways and setting tyres on fire. The electricity crisis has also raised concerns about how the government is managing the country's vast oil supply, a key source of income for the country.

"We are desperate. We cannot understand how a country so rich in resources can be practically left in the dark," said Patricia Cueva, a lawyer from Maracaibo, the capital of oil-rich Zulia state.

"We cannot rest. We cannot work. Our children cry."

articles.title: A beautiful Himalayan bird is changing its voice due to human activity, research shows
articles.summary: A sharp increase in human activity is affecting the way the Himalayan monal lives and communicates, studies show.
articles.body:
A sharp increase in human activity is having an impact on the way a Himalayan bird lives and communicates, two studies by Indian researchers have found.

The monal, a pheasant native to Himalayan mountain forests, is deeply woven into the region's cultural, folklore and identity. The eye-catching monal - the male has distinctive green, blue and copper feathers - is the state bird of India's Uttarakhand state and the national bird of Nepal, reflecting its cultural significance across the Himalayas.

But studies show that infrastructure development and tourism are squeezing its habitat, while increasing noise is altering how it communicates with potential mates and rivals.

Researchers from Uttarakhand conducted two separate studies over five years which flagged key threats to the bird.

One study found that the birds are forced to move higher in the mountains as their natural habitat in the alpine meadows above the tree line get crowded. The other says the monal is changing its pitch to cut through human noise in a busy valley.

"These two studies give a useful warning for other more vulnerable species - if the monal is forced to change both its voice and its address, how are the more sensitive species responding?" says Vishal Singh, an environmental practitioner working on ecology and climate issues in the Himalayas.

Dr Rajeev Lochan, lead researcher of both studies, told the BBC that they chose to study the monal as the bird has a narrow habitat range - it moves seasonally between the lower montane zone - an ecological belt found on the lower slopes of the mountains - and high-elevation alpine zones. This, he says, makes it a key indicator of ecosystem health in the north-western Himalayas.

"If the species is facing issues on this particular landscape, there might be a chance that the ecological disturbances are affecting other birds too," said Lochan.

The monal, researchers say, can be seen as a stand-in for the health of a fragile Himalayan ecosystem pushed to a tipping point due to unregulated tourism and heavy urbanisation.

While the region has always drawn tourists, trekkers and researchers given its scenic landscape and biodiversity, rapid infrastructure expansion in the past decade has made more places accessible, increasing footfall and disrupting the wildlife. This, coupled with mounting human pressures, suggests that climate change is emerging as another major threat to the region's already vulnerable biodiversity.

"There are a lot of factors at play but at a broader level, the problem is that the economic development of the region is not aligned to its ecological integrity," Singh said.

According to the first study, climate change is projected to continue shrinking and destabilising the Himalayan monal's habitat across the Indian Himalayas through 2100 under multiple climate scenarios.

Currently, the birds are found in alpine meadows, located high in the mountains above the forests, which form some of the Himalayas' most important seasonal grazing and biodiversity-rich habitats.

The researchers modelled how climate change could shift the monal's suitable habitat across the Indian Himalayan region in the states of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. It was based on the kind of global climate models and emissions scenarios used for assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN's climate science unit.

"These birds are now slowly moving upwards in the Himalayas as the snow is melting and vegetation is growing, making the area accessible to them. They are anyway being pushed upwards as their natural habitats in alpine meadows are being encroached upon by humans," Lochan said.

The model assumes that the bird needs the current climate set-up that exists in alpine meadows in the future too, a reasonable but not certain assumption.

The birds' seasonal migration may become increasingly difficult as changes in climate may force them to move to higher elevations on hills, to smaller and fragmented areas. Their population would be scattered in disconnected pockets, which reduces chances of breeding between groups and increases their risks of long-term decline or local extinction, which is already a threat, the study says.

The second study, also conducted by Lochan, Dinesh Kumar Sharma and Anand Kumar, who work at the Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, focuses on the bird's behavioural changes. They conducted the study in two valleys in Kedarnath Musk Deer Sanctuary in Uttarakhand - at Chopta, a tourist spot with busy traffic and visitors, and the largely quiet Madmaheshwar.

They recorded more than 700 monal calls across both sites using microphones and passive recording devices and then measured pitch, call length and background noise levels for a year from April 2023.

Birds in noisy environments consistently produced calls with significantly higher peak frequencies compared with those in quieter habitats, the study said.

The researchers found subtle changes in the monal's pitch that could be picked up by recording devices but might go unnoticed by the human ear.

"This does not mean that the species has undergone a permanent or evolutionary change in its vocal frequency; rather, our findings suggest behavioural flexibility in response to different acoustic environments," Lochan said.

Compared with the birds in Madmaheshwar valley, the monal in Chopta also produced shorter call durations likely to cut through low-frequency human noise from traffic and tourist footfall.

Bird calls are one of the most sophisticated forms of sound-based communication in the natural world, and significant changes can interfere with, among other things, their mating success.

"When a species must raise its pitch to be heard over tourist traffic, or climb higher as meadows turn crowded, it reveals how human pressure is rewriting the rules of life in the Himalaya," says Anjal Prakash, a public policy professor at FLAME University and contributor to IPCC reports.

Lochan says he and his team consider this a preliminary study and hope to expand the scope and depth of it.

The research comes with the caveat that it is not conclusive on ecological consequences, and more research is needed. But together, the two studies signal broader ecological stress across the Himalayas.

"In listening to the monal, we hear the Himalayas asking for space, silence and care," says Prakash.

articles.title: 'That nagging feeling of dread': Is 'hang-xiety' a real thing?
articles.summary: For some, a hangover can start an anxious spiral. We spoke to experts about the reasons why.
articles.body:
You wake up. Your head throbs. Then comes the second wave: a low, gnawing horror at what you might have done.

You scroll back through last night's messages, certain you said something wrong.

You replay conversations worried you offended someone, embarrassed yourself, or both.

"It's that nagging feeling of dread," says 25-year old Eleanor Tobin who works in marketing and events in London.

"If the day starts with me doing a checklist of my things - panically checking I have my bag, my phone - I know the anxiety is going to seep into everything I do beyond just reliving the night before."

This is hang-xiety, a name coined in social slang a decade ago, for the anxiety that can accompany a hangover.

"Alcohol affects the body in many ways - the brain, sleep, hormones and nervous system - that all help explain why a night out drinking can be followed by an excessively anxious morning," says Celia Morgan, professor of psychopharmacology at the University of Exeter.

Alcohol affects two chemical messengers in the brain: GABA and glutamate.

GABA acts a little like the brain's braking system, reducing nerve-cell activity. Glutamate is involved in excitation and alertness.

Alcohol enhances the effects of GABA and suppresses some glutamate activity, helping to produce that familiar feeling of relaxation and lowered inhibitions.

But the brain is constantly trying to restore balance. As alcohol wears off, the nervous system can swing towards greater alertness and arousal.

This can trigger anxiety. "Everything is always 100% worse in my mind when you have a hangover than in reality," says Tobin.

A 2023 study of over 5,000 students from the UK and the Netherlands, concluded that 18.3% reported symptoms of anxiety when hungover.

Studies also suggest that not everyone gets hang-xiety, and the level of anxiety does not neatly correlate with how much you drink the night before. Existing psychological characteristics – and potentially genetics – appear to play a part.

In 2019 researchers at the University of Exeter studied this in 97 social drinkers.

Those who drank reported a spike in anxiety the following day compared with a control group who stayed sober. The effect was strongest in people who had scored highly for shyness before drinking.

Morgan's research found that shy drinkers often felt less anxious during the evening itself. Alcohol was doing exactly what they hoped, quieting social nerves, but the rebound came the next day.

"Shy people were hit even harder the next morning, with hugely elevated anxiety markers, especially when compared with those that weren't naturally shy," says Morgan.

Innocuous moments get reinterpreted as embarrassing. A perfectly normal joke becomes, in the retelling inside your own head, a terrible mistake.

The anxious spiral can outlast the physical symptoms, because it feeds on itself: worry disrupts thinking, and disrupted thinking produces more worry.

If Tobin has been out Friday and Saturday night, by Sunday that spiral can become overwhelming.

"Suddenly taking the underground can feel like a challenge - normal stuff feels hard when you got a really bad case of the 'Sunday scaries' triggered by two hangovers in a row," she says.

You may have fallen asleep quickly after drinking, but that doesn't mean you've had a good night's sleep, researchers warn.

Alcohol disrupts sleep, including the pattern of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which is important for emotional regulation. Wake up dehydrated and sleep-deprived, and your ability to cope with anxious thoughts is already reduced.

"Light and broken sleep means you wake feeling on edge," says Dr Alanna Hare, President of the British Sleep Society.

"Even if you have eight hours in bed, you haven't had a proper night's sleep, and a tired brain is more reactive to worry."

The advice from researchers is unglamorous but consistent. Moderating alcohol intake matters more than any remedy taken afterwards. Drinking water between alcoholic drinks can help, so can eating during your night out.

UK guidelines recommend no more than 14 units a week, the equivalent to six pints of beer or six medium glasses of wine, spread across several days.

Alcohol Change UK director Andrew Misell says it's important not to reach for alcohol to manage or mask stress.

"Alcohol turns into a depressant and can exacerbate all sorts of problems with our physical and mental health," he says, advising people to see their GP if they are struggling with the spiral. Talking to a close friend can also be a good starting point.

And perhaps the most useful trick if you are suffering with hang-xiety is to reframe the thoughts. Recognising hang-xiety as a temporary state, rather than proof that something has gone horribly wrong socially, can blunt its power.

The dread is real. The catastrophe it points to usually isn't.

So the next time the Sunday morning spiral sets in, remember it may simply be your brain and body trying to regain balance after alcohol.

articles.title: UK weather: Midweek to bring coldest night of the autumn so far
articles.summary: The first frost of the season is expected for some places this week as colder, Arctic air moves across the UK bringing a dip in temperatures. But how cold will it get and how long will the chillier spell last? Sarah Keith-Lucas takes a look.
articles.body:
After a spell of unusually warm weather, UK temperatures are set to tumble with the coldest night of autumn so far arriving by midweek.

Wednesday night will bring the first frost of the season to some places, as colder air arrives from the Arctic.

In some areas, minimum temperatures could be just a degree or two above freezing by dawn on Thursday.

Along with the plummeting temperatures, some much-needed rainfall is on the way for England and Wales.

So far this autumn, the jet stream - which determines what sort of air mass affects the UK - has been sitting to the north.

This has allowed mild south or south-westerly winds to flow, particularly across the southern half of the British Isles.

This week, however, the jet stream will start to sink further south, allowing the winds to turn more northerly and introduce a colder air mass.

While it will feel significantly colder compared to recent weeks, especially in the south, temperatures will actually be near normal for the time of year or perhaps just a little below.

Afternoon highs on Wednesday will be around 12C to 14C in Northern Ireland and Scotland and 14C to 16C in England and Wales.

Whilst the northern half of the UK has already seen temperatures near the seasonal average this month, it has consistently been several degrees above average in the south, with somewhere reaching above 20C every day since 11 June.

By the overnight hours, temperatures will be unseasonably low with a noticeable chill first thing on Thursday.

Minimum temperatures at dawn will be around 5 to 7C for most places, but the coolest areas in northern and eastern England as well as eastern Scotland could be just a degree or two above freezing.

A touch of frost is likely on grass and car windscreens here.

In addition to the autumn chill, much-needed rain will spread across England and Wales from midweek.

Wednesday will start cloudy and wet as a frontal system slowly drifts eastwards.

Whilst sunshine will return to many places in the afternoon, rain is expected to linger for most of the day in East Anglia and the far south-east.

Southern and eastern England, where it has been especially dry lately, could receive around 20 to 30mm.

This would equate to up to half a month's rainfall in just 24 hours.

Nearly three quarters of England and all of Wales are still in drought .

The Environment Agency has previously said that 20% more rainfall than average is needed for at least seven months before all areas will be out of drought status.

The chilly feel to the weather will continue into Thursday, with maximum temperatures between around 11 to 16C north to south.

With plenty of dry and bright weather though, it may well feel pleasant in the afternoon sunshine for many.

By Friday, temperatures will be on the rise once more.

Westerly winds will push milder air across England and Wales, where 20C could again be reached in the east.

Further north, no frost is expected by Friday dawn and afternoon highs will peak in the mid teens Celsius.

Keep up to date with the longer range forecast in BBC Weather's Monthly Outlook .
